Neonatal female grey-headed flying foxes weigh approximately 90 grams [Wwb = approximately 90 grams] at parturition, a modest birth mass that reflects the energetic constraints of producing a single offspring during the austral spring. This initial wet weight is considerably lower than the ultimate adult female body mass, which reaches around 1000 grams [Wwi = around 1000 grams] in mature individuals, indicating a substantial post-natal growth trajectory that spans many months. Field studies conducted in southeastern Queensland have documented that newborn pups cling tightly to their mothers' ventral fur, remaining continuously attached for the first several weeks of life while they rely exclusively on milk for nourishment. The relatively low neonatal mass compared to the asymptotic adult size suggests that most somatic development occurs after birth, a pattern common among large-bodied pteropodid bats. Lactating females must therefore sustain high rates of energy transfer to their dependent young, a demand that intensifies as the offspring approaches the weaning stage. Reproductive output is limited to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and the maximum reproduction rate has been estimated at one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, specifically at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].

Gestation in the grey-headed flying fox proceeds over a period of 190 days [tg = 190 days] when measured at the species' typical core body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], reflecting the protracted embryogenesis characteristic of large frugivorous bats. This relatively lengthy intrauterine development, encompassing syncytial organogenesis and foetal growth, is followed by the emergence of a single, well-developed neonate that is capable of immediate teat attachment and sustained suckling. The duration of gestation is comparable to that reported for other members of the genus Pteropus, though slight variation exists across populations depending on local climatic conditions and maternal nutritional status. After parturition, the nursing juvenile remains dependent on its mother's milk for an extended period, gradually transitioning to solid foods as it matures. Weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the onset of full nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 130 days after birth [tx = approximately 130 days after birth] under the same thermoregulatory regime of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], a timing that aligns with the availability of peak fruit abundance in late summer.

Females of Pteropus poliocephalus reach sexual maturity and produce their first litter at 540 days after birth [tp = 540 days after birth], a milestone attained under the species' regulated body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This age at first reproduction, approximately 18 months, represents a relatively rapid maturation schedule for a mammal of its size, allowing young females to contribute to population recruitment within their second year of life. The timing of first parturition is closely tied to the seasonal availability of nectar and fruit resources, which in eastern Australia peak during the warmer months and provide the energetic foundation for successful lactation and offspring rearing. Sub-adult females typically give birth to a single pup, consistent with the species' invariant litter size of one offspring per reproductive event. The maximum reproduction rate, reflecting the upper limit of annual fecundity for this bat, has been estimated at a single pup per year under the ambient thermal conditions that sustain its physiological processes at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C].

Maximum longevity in wild populations of the grey-headed flying fox has been documented to reach approximately 20.6 years [am = approximately 20.6 years] under the species' typical core temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], placing it among the longer-lived bat species relative to its body mass. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 7,519 days, is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many pteropodid bats, which combine low annual reproductive output with high adult survival. Mark-recapture studies conducted across multiple roost sites in New South Wales and Queensland have revealed that individuals regularly survive for over a decade, with the oldest verified record exceeding two decades. This remarkable longevity is supported by a suite of life-history traits including late maturity, a single offspring per year, and extended parental care through a prolonged weaning period. The sustained reproductive value of older females, who continue to produce pups well into their second decade, underscores the importance of adult survival for population persistence. Comparative analyses with other members of the Chiroptera indicate that Pteropus poliocephalus exhibits a longevity that exceeds allometric predictions based on body mass alone, suggesting the evolution of enhanced cellular maintenance mechanisms.

The ecological role of Pteropus poliocephalus as a keystone pollinator and seed disperser in eastern Australian forests is intimately linked to its life-history schedule. Juveniles, after completing the post-weaning transition to solid foods, begin foraging independently within their natal roost's foraging range, gradually learning the spatial distribution of flowering Eucalyptus and fruiting rainforest trees. The period between weaning and sexual maturity, spanning roughly one year, represents a critical phase during which young bats must acquire the navigational knowledge and dietary flexibility necessary for survival. Mortality during this juvenile stage is elevated compared to adults, with predation by powerful owls and lacerating encounters with barbed-wire fences representing significant threats. As adults, these flying foxes form large diurnal colonies that can number in the tens of thousands, facilitating information transfer about ephemeral food resources. The species' ability to travel over 50 kilometers in a single night's foraging bout enables long-distance pollen transfer across fragmented landscapes. Conservation efforts increasingly focus on protecting maternity roosts during the spring birthing season, ensuring that the interplay between neonatal mass, gestation length, and weaning timing continues to function effectively in the face of habitat loss and climate change.
